title: Maximum Gap
description: Find the maximum gap between adjacent values in sorted order, in linear time, using a pigeonhole-guaranteed bucket sort.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, return the maximum difference between two successive elements in its sorted form. If the array has fewer than 2 elements, return 0. The solution should run in linear time and use linear extra space.

blocks.caption: Bucketing values into n-1 equal-width ranges guarantees at least one empty bucket, which is exactly where the maximum gap must occur.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (non-negative integers)"],["Output","The maximum gap between adjacent values in sorted order"],["Constraint","Must run in O(n) time and O(n) space, ruling out a comparison sort"]]}

blocks.text: The linear-time requirement rules out comparison-based sorting (which needs O(n log n)). This is the classic signal for a BUCKET SORT style approach: divide the value range into n-1 equal-width buckets, and by the pigeonhole principle, at least one bucket must be empty, guaranteeing the maximum gap spans BETWEEN buckets, never within one.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This pigeonhole-guaranteed-empty-bucket trick is a specific, elegant application of bucket sort, distinct from the more general "counting sort for small integer ranges" seen in problems like Height Checker.

Picture dividing the full range of values into n-1 equal-sized pigeonholes. With n numbers spread across only n-1 holes, at least one hole is guaranteed to end up empty, by the pigeonhole principle. Since each hole is narrower than the width spanned by any guaranteed-empty hole, the true maximum gap can never be found strictly within a single hole. It is therefore always found by comparing the smallest value in one hole to the largest value in the previous non-empty hole.

blocks.caption: A guaranteed-empty pigeonhole means the true maximum gap always spans between buckets.

items: Find min and max of the array; if they are equal, the answer is trivially 0.
Divide the range [min, max] into n-1 buckets of equal width (rounded up), so at least one bucket is guaranteed empty.
Track only the min and max WITHIN each non-empty bucket; the maximum gap is the largest difference between a bucket's min and the PREVIOUS non-empty bucket's max.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Scanning non-empty buckets in order (0, 2, 4): gap between bucket 0's max (3) and bucket 2's min (6) is 3; gap between bucket 2's max (6) and bucket 4's min (9) is 3. The maximum gap is 3, matching the expected output.
The direct approach sorts the array with a comparison sort and scans adjacent pairs. This is correct and simple, but takes O(n log n) time, violating the linear-time requirement.

Bucket sort with the pigeonhole guarantee achieves the same result in O(n): since at least one bucket must be empty (n numbers spread across n-1 buckets), the true maximum gap can never occur strictly within a single bucket (each bucket's width is smaller than what the guaranteed empty bucket forces), so only min/max PER bucket needs tracking, not a full sort.
Sort the array with a comparison sort and scan adjacent pairs for the maximum gap.

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: This does not satisfy the problem's explicit linear-time requirement, even though it is otherwise a perfectly correct and simple solution.

Compute min and max, then divide the range into n-1 equal-width buckets. Track only the min and max value within each bucket (never a full sorted list per bucket). Scan buckets left to right, computing the gap between each non-empty bucket's min and the previous non-empty bucket's max, tracking the overall maximum.

items: Compute bucket size and count so that n-1 buckets guarantee at least one is empty.
Assign each number to its bucket, tracking only that bucket's min/max, O(n).
Scan buckets once, comparing consecutive non-empty buckets, O(bucketCount).

codes.python:
def maximum_gap(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    if n < 2:
        return 0

    min_val, max_val = min(nums), max(nums)
    if min_val == max_val:
        return 0

    bucket_size = max(1, (max_val - min_val) // (n - 1))
    bucket_count = (max_val - min_val) // bucket_size + 1
    bucket_min = [float('inf')] * bucket_count
    bucket_max = [float('-inf')] * bucket_count

    for num in nums:
        idx = (num - min_val) // bucket_size
        bucket_min[idx] = min(bucket_min[idx], num)
        bucket_max[idx] = max(bucket_max[idx], num)

    max_gap = 0
    prev_max = min_val
    for i in range(bucket_count):
        if bucket_min[i] == float('inf'):
            continue
        max_gap = max(max_gap, bucket_min[i] - prev_max)
        prev_max = bucket_max[i]

    return max_gap


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(maximum_gap([3, 6, 9, 1]))
    print(maximum_gap([10]))

items: When a linear-time constraint rules out comparison sorting, look for a pigeonhole or counting-based bucketing trick specific to the problem.
Sizing buckets so there are fewer buckets than elements guarantees at least one empty bucket, which is exactly where the answer (a maximum gap) must be found.
Only the min and max within each bucket ever need tracking, not the full contents, since the maximum gap can never occur strictly inside a single bucket under this sizing.

blocks.text: Maximum Gap is solved with a pigeonhole-based bucket sort: dividing the value range into n-1 equal-width buckets guarantees at least one is empty, meaning the maximum gap always occurs between buckets. Tracking only each bucket's min and max, then scanning consecutive non-empty buckets, finds the answer in O(n) time and space, satisfying the problem's linear-time requirement.
